_notes.usage: Copy this file to config.json and fill in real values. config.json is gitignored-by-convention and should never be committed (it holds credentials).
_notes.model_path / paddleocr model dirs: model_path (the YOLO weights, e.g. best.pt) and alpr.paddleocr_det_model_dir/paddleocr_rec_model_dir/paddleocr_cls_model_dir are all resolved relative to the FOLDER config.json ACTUALLY LOADED FROM, not the code's location -- so by default everything lives together in one folder. det and rec are REAL, required models -- place the actual downloaded files there (flat, no subfolders: inference.pdmodel/inference.pdiparams/inference.pdiparams.info). cls (angle classifier) is different: PaddleOCR's constructor unconditionally tries to download it regardless of use_angle_cls, but the code always passes use_angle_cls=false, and confirmed from paddleocr's own source, the classifier object that would actually READ those files is only ever instantiated when use_angle_cls=true -- so cls's file CONTENT never matters, only its existence. The service creates empty placeholder files there itself on first run (see worker.py's ensure_cls_placeholder) specifically so a machine with no route to paddleocr.bj.bcebos.com -- e.g. behind a corporate proxy blocking that download's HTTPS tunnel, a real failure this was written to fix -- never needs a real cls model at all. You never need to place cls files yourself; if you see it trying to download anyway, delete any partial/leftover file in paddleocr_models/cls first, then restart.
_notes.mqtt.trigger_enabled / http_trigger: Two independent, combinable trigger sources. mqtt.trigger_enabled (default true) subscribes to the VCA event topics below as before. http_trigger.enabled (default false) instead/additionally runs an HTTP server (served by waitress, a production WSGI server -- not Flask's dev server) that a camera's own alarm task (e.g. a Bosch dome's built-in 'HTTP notification' action) calls directly on a rule trigger, bypassing Genetec/MQTT for the trigger itself. MQTT stays connected and is always used to publish results either way -- disabling mqtt.trigger_enabled only stops it from subscribing. At least one of the two must be enabled. See the 'http_trigger' block below for its own settings.
_notes.http_trigger.port/threads: port must match whatever the camera's Alarm Task Editor HttpCommand is configured to send to (its Port(...) value) -- a mismatch means the request never arrives. threads is waitress's worker pool size; the default of 4 is plenty for this endpoint's workload (a handful of alarm hits per truck, each just a dict lookup + queue put). GET /healthz always returns 200 if the server is up, independent of ALPR's own health, for a process supervisor/load balancer to poll.
_notes.http_trigger SSL: If the camera's HttpCommand has SSL(false) (the default in Bosch's Alarm Task Editor), plain HTTP is all that's needed -- nothing else to configure. Only if a camera is set to SSL(true) would this need a certificate (e.g. a self-signed cert passed to waitress, or a reverse proxy terminating TLS in front of it) -- not set up here since it isn't needed for SSL(false).
_notes.snapshot: Every camera is pulled via a single HTTP GET to its snapshot endpoint (e.g. a Bosch dome's /snap.jpg), authenticated with HTTP Digest, using one common username/password for ALL cameras -- there's no per-camera override and no RTSP/Genetec path anymore (removed in favor of this). During a collection window the service polls this endpoint repeatedly (as fast as the HTTP round trip allows, or paced by poll_interval_ms) instead of decoding a continuous video stream. Chosen because trigger events here are trucks crawling in slowly, not fast drive-bys, so RTSP's much higher frame rate wasn't needed to catch a good shot.
_notes.snapshot.url_template: Default matches a Bosch FLEXIDOME 3000i/5000i's snapshot path: http://ip:80/snap.jpg. Confirm on your specific unit's web UI under RTSP/streaming (or HTTP) settings if snapshots fail or come back low-res.
_notes.alpr.expected_frame_width/height: Set to your camera's real sensor resolution (e.g. a 5MP camera is commonly 2592x1944) to catch the snapshot endpoint unexpectedly serving a lower-res image than the camera's actual sensor. Leave both null to disable the check.
_notes.logging.level: Text log verbosity: DEBUG / INFO / WARNING / ERROR. Independent of alpr.diagnostics_mode below, but diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting' forces this to DEBUG regardless of what's set here.
_notes.alpr.diagnostics_mode: 'basic' (default): saves the first fetched frame + its ROI crop, the OCR-attempted crops, and the OCR-prep images -- fine for normal operation. 'troubleshooting': all of that PLUS every fetched frame (full image and ROI), the ROI annotated with every box the model returned (green=kept, red=rejected-by-size/position, orange=rejected-as-duplicate, with the rejection reason labeled), and every kept candidate crop saved the instant it's found, not just the ones that got OCR'd -- and forces logging to DEBUG. Use this to see WHY, e.g., ocr_attempts stays at 0 (wrong ROI vs. camera framing? model detecting nothing at all vs. detecting boxes but all getting filtered out?). Generates a lot more files per event -- meant to be turned on temporarily while diagnosing, then switched back to 'basic'.
_notes.alpr.max_ocr_attempts / collection_timeo: The first detected plate box in ANY frame is the trigger to start OCRing immediately -- best-scoring candidate first within a frame, continuing across subsequent frames -- and the whole collection stops the instant one produces a plate that passes plate_text.is_valid(), rather than waiting out the full collection window and voting across whatever showed up. max_ocr_attempts caps how many OCR calls one collection window will make (across all frames, not per frame) before giving up; collection_timeout is a wall-clock backstop on top of that (e.g. a truck that never presents a readable plate). There is no fallback vote if the budget runs out with nothing valid -- the result is NO_VALID_PLATE, and every individual attempt (valid or not) is still in the audit result.json's 'reads' array for forensics. A near-duplicate crop (the same plate, barely moved between two consecutive frames) does not consume a fresh attempt -- it's skipped before OCR runs, same duplicate_diff_threshold/duplicate_resize_* comparison as before.
_notes.alpr.upper_half_fraction: A detected box is rejected as 'upper_half' if its vertical center sits above this fraction of the ROI's height (0.45 = reject anything in the top 45%). Meant to filter false positives from cab signage/mounting hardware above the real plate -- but if your camera's mounting angle puts the real plate legitimately high in the ROI, this will silently discard correct detections (confirmed via diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting': the model boxed the plate correctly but it was labeled upper_half). Lower it (e.g. 0.15) or set to 0 to disable the check entirely if that happens.
_notes.alpr.plate_crop_padding_pct: Expands each detected box by this percent of its own width/height (each side) before cropping for OCR, clamped to the ROI's bounds. Fixes a real observed failure: a slightly undersized YOLO box clips a character off the plate's edge -- confirmed via two adjacent, overlapping detections that each only captured half a plate ('HR47E' / 'E4812', sharing the boundary 'E', for what was actually 'HR47E4812'). Set to 0 to disable; raise it if plates are still getting clipped, lower it if crops start including too much surrounding clutter.
_notes.event_filter: Trigger events carry a VCA classification per detected object, e.g. Data.Object.Object.Appearance.Class.Type = {"#text": "Vehicle", "@Likelihood": 0.91}. Only events with a detection matching one of class_types (case-insensitive) at or above min_likelihood are queued for ALPR -- everything else (Person/Bicycle detections, low-confidence hits, events with no classified object) is discarded before a single snapshot is fetched. Tune min_likelihood against the values your camera actually reports (0.91 in the sample payload this was built from).
_notes.event_filter.class_types (disabling): Set class_types to an empty array, [], to disable this filter entirely and queue EVERY line-crossing event regardless of classification -- min_likelihood is then ignored too. Do not just delete min_likelihood or set it to 0/null while leaving class_types non-empty -- the event still has to match one of class_types first, so that alone would not stop filtering.
_notes.alpr.publish_no_valid_plate: true (default): every trigger gets an MQTT reply regardless of read success -- a NO_VALID_PLATE collection still publishes {..., "truck_number": "UNKNOWN", "status": "NO_VALID_PLATE", ...} so a downstream consumer knows the event was processed, not just silence. (truck_number is never null -- see alpr.unknown_plate_value.) The audit folder (result.json/event.json) is always written either way. Camera/system errors (CAMERA_UNREACHABLE, CAMERA_CONFIG_ERROR, FRAME_SIZE_ERROR, ERROR) are unaffected and always publish regardless of this setting. Set false to only publish actual successful reads -- note that doing so also means a no-read visit produces no message at all, which is the one case where "always reports a truck number" stops applying.
_notes.mqtt enter/leave (filtering): Entering and leaving are two independent triggers, each its own MQTT subscription -- which rule/event types reach this service at all is decided by these topic filters (MQTT wildcards), not by any code-side filtering. Confirmed against real captured events for the SAME tracked object (ObjectId) a few seconds apart: enter_subscribe_topic matches 'Camera_Events/AR-H6/onvif-ej/RuleEngine/LineDetector/Crossed/&1/Entering field 2' (event_type=LineDetector; this same topic shape also covers plain 'Crossing line N' rules), and leave_subscribe_topic matches 'Camera_Events/AR-H6/onvif-ej/RuleEngine/ObjectTrack/Aggregation/&1/Leaving field 3' (event_type=ObjectTrack) -- '+' matches exactly one topic segment, '#' matches all remaining segments (only valid at the end, absorbs the varying '&1/<free text>' suffix). The two are structurally distinct (LineDetector/Crossed vs ObjectTrack/Aggregation) so there's no overlap between them.
_notes.mqtt enter/leave (results): Each direction publishes to its own topic (enter_result_topic_prefix/<bay> or leave_result_topic_prefix/<bay>) with a lean payload -- bay, direction, truck_number, confidence, status, event_time/ocr_time -- so a downstream gate/dock system can subscribe to entries and exits separately without parsing the fuller record. The complete detail (every OCR read, collection stats, rejection reasons) is still written to the audit folder's result.json regardless.
_notes.mqtt.bay_segment_index: 0-based position of the bay name within the subscribe topics, e.g. 1 for 'Camera_Events/<bay>/...'. Shared by both enter and leave since they use the same layout; adjust if yours differs.
_notes.bay_monitor: A separate, optional feature from the enter/leave ALPR pipeline above -- off by default (enabled: false). Continuously round-robins every enabled camera (independent of MQTT/HTTP triggers) looking for presence via a plain frame-diff against the ROI's last-seen-empty state -- deliberately NOT the ALPR plate model, since a bay is occupied or not regardless of whether a plate happens to be visible (a reversed-in trailer's plate usually faces away from the dock camera entirely). Once a bay's scene changes it's 'zoomed in': every classify_interval_sec (default 60s) a frame is sent to a local Ollama-hosted vision model and the reply (one of status_values) is published to mqtt.bay_status_topic_prefix + '/<bay>'. After empty_debounce_count consecutive 'empty' replies it reverts to baseline scanning. ollama_model has NO working default -- it must be set to a vision-capable model tag you've actually pulled locally (`ollama pull <tag>`), and the service fails fast at startup if enabled without one set, rather than silently misclassifying everything.
_notes.bay_monitor.baseline_scan_interval_ms: Pacing between each camera checked in the round-robin (applies whether or not anything was found) -- keeps the scanner from hammering every camera back-to-back with zero gap. Does not apply to the classify_interval_sec cadence of a zoomed-in bay's LLM calls, which is separately paced.
_notes.bay_monitor.reference_images: Optional few-shot exemplars sent alongside every classification call, e.g. [{"path": "reference_images/empty.jpg", "label": "empty"}, {"path": "reference_images/door_open.jpg", "label": "occupied (bay door open)"}]. Paths resolve relative to config.json's directory, like model_path. Loaded once at startup, not re-read per call -- a missing file is logged and skipped, not fatal. Helps most on real ambiguous cases a text-only prompt undersells, e.g. an open bay/cargo door that can otherwise get misread as empty or throw off the model.
_notes.bay_state_engine: Off by default; depends entirely on bay_monitor also being enabled (fails startup otherwise). When on, it becomes the authority for enter/leave direction and timing INSTEAD of the MQTT/HTTP trigger source: bay_monitor's own empty->occupied transition enqueues an ALPR read via the normal Worker pool, and (unlike a one-shot trigger) keeps retrying every time bay_monitor reclassifies the bay as still occupied, until a read actually succeeds -- so a bad read caused by e.g. a bay/cargo door being open doesn't cost the whole visit's identity, just that one attempt. occupied->empty then publishes the leave result using whatever plate got confirmed at ANY point during the stay (there's no fresh camera read at that instant to attempt, since 'empty' means the truck's no longer in frame). If mqtt.trigger_enabled or http_trigger.enabled are ALSO on at the same time, both paths independently decide enter/leave for the same bays -- a startup warning (not a hard failure) flags this, since it usually means redundant or conflicting publishes; turn the old trigger(s) off if bay_state_engine is meant to be the sole source of truth. State is in-memory only -- a restart loses any truck currently mid-visit.
_notes.mqtt.bay_state_topic_prefix: Where bay_state_engine publishes its LIVE per-bay session ('/<bay>' appended) -- {bay, occupancy_status, activity, open, direction, plate, confidence, read_attempts, timestamp} -- on every state change: arrival (session opens), a plate getting confirmed, and departure (session closes). occupancy_status is 'occupied'/'empty' and activity is bay_monitor's raw classification word (may be finer, e.g. 'loading') -- included here, not just on mqtt.bay_notification_topic_prefix, since this is the topic most likely already being watched. 'open' is the session-lifecycle boolean (true from arrival until departure) -- functionally the same signal as occupancy_status, kept for anything that already reads it. This is separate from, and unconditional unlike, mqtt.enter_result_topic_prefix/leave_result_topic_prefix -- those only ever fire once per visit (on departure) and are suppressed entirely by alpr.publish_no_valid_plate=false when nothing was confirmed; this topic always fires regardless, since its purpose is showing the engine is alive and reacting, not delivering a final result to a downstream gate/dock system. Only published if bay_state_engine.enabled is true.
_notes.mqtt.bay_notification_topic_prefix: Where bay_state_engine publishes a RICH notification ('/<bay>' appended) whenever bay_monitor's activity classification actually CHANGES (idle->loading, empty->occupied, etc) -- {bay, occupancy_status, activity, truck_number, comment, image_base64, timestamp}. occupancy_status is 'occupied'/'empty' (bay_monitor's own occupied/departed interpretation, honoring empty_debounce_count); activity is the raw classification word (may be finer, e.g. 'loading'/'unloading'/'idle'); truck_number is whatever this visit's plate is confirmed as SO FAR (or alpr.unknown_plate_value if not yet/never confirmed) -- captured before any session reset, so a departure notification still names the truck that just left; comment is the vision model's own free-text description (see bay_monitor.classification_prompt's STATUS:/COMMENT: format); image_base64 is the exact frame it was shown. Fires on the bay's very first-ever classification too (a 'change' from unknown). Requires bay_state_engine.enabled -- only it tracks truck_number, so bay_monitor alone has nothing to report here.
_notes.bay_state_engine.save_state_csv: Overwrites audit/bay_state.csv with a one-row-per-bay snapshot of current state (bay_status, session_open, direction, plate, confidence, read_attempts, last_updated) on every classification AND every plate confirmation -- always the current table, not an append-only log, so the file stays small and just opening it (Excel, Notepad, anything) shows the latest state at a glance, no MQTT client or subscription needed. last_updated moving is itself a health signal: if it stops advancing, bay_monitor/bay_state_engine has stalled. Written via a temp-file-then-rename so a reader never sees a half-written row. Requires bay_state_engine.enabled.
_notes.thresholds (all in config now): Every numeric decision boundary the code makes is a config value with no separate code-level default of its own beyond what's documented here -- nothing requires a code change to retune. alpr.yolo_conf_threshold is the minimum YOLO box confidence for a plate detection to be considered at all (Ultralytics' own unstated default is 0.25 if not set). bay_monitor's own baseline presence check is unrelated to this model or threshold -- see bay_monitor.presence_diff_* below. alpr.score_weights (plus score_area_norm/score_sharpness_norm) control how multiple candidate crops from one collection window get ranked against each other; alpr.duplicate_resize_width/_height/duplicate_diff_threshold control when two crops are treated as the same sighting rather than voted on twice; alpr.ocr_prep_target_height/ocr_prep_padding control how a crop is resized/bordered before OCR; alpr.max_consecutive_fetch_failures/fetch_failure_backoff_sec control when a collection window gives up on a camera that's not responding.
_notes.alpr.unknown_plate_value: Every published result carries a truck_number STRING, never null -- anything short of a valid read reports this placeholder ('UNKNOWN' by default) instead, so a downstream consumer never has to null-check the field. The 'status' field (SUCCESS / NO_VALID_PLATE / CAMERA_UNREACHABLE / CAMERA_CONFIG_ERROR / FRAME_SIZE_ERROR / ERROR) is what distinguishes a genuine read from the placeholder. Keep it to something no real plate could be -- it must not satisfy the Indian-plate patterns in plate_text.py, or a placeholder could be mistaken for a real read. Note this is about the VALUE reported; alpr.publish_no_valid_plate separately controls whether a no-read result is published at all (leave it true if you want an update on every trigger regardless of outcome). The audit result.json additionally keeps 'final_plate' (same value as truck_number on SUCCESS, null otherwise) and the full 'reads' array -- every individual OCR attempt, valid or not -- so the placeholder never hides forensic detail.
_notes.bay_monitor.empty_status / classify_regi: empty_status names which entry of status_values means 'nothing is there'; it drives both bay_monitor's revert-to-baseline debounce and bay_state_engine's occupied set (everything that isn't it), so a custom status_values vocabulary works end to end without either hardcoding the literal 'empty'. classify_region picks which pixels the vision model judges: 'full_frame' (default) shows it the whole bay -- cargo, forklifts, doors, which is what the activity vocabulary is really about -- but a truck in an ADJACENT bay that's also in shot can then drive this bay's status (and, with bay_state_engine on, open a session on the wrong bay). Set it to 'roi' to restrict classification to the same cameras.json roi presence detection uses, removing that cross-talk at the cost of a much narrower view (the roi is framed for plates, not for watching cargo movement). Use 'roi' if your bays overlap in frame.
_notes.service.num_workers/queue_max: num_workers is roughly 'how many trucks this instance can process at once' -- each Worker thread owns its own loaded YOLO+PaddleOCR models (~2GB RAM apiece), so this is a memory/CPU sizing knob, not just a throughput one. queue_max caps how many pending jobs JobBus holds before it starts dropping new ones instead of growing unbounded.
_notes.alpr.max_read_attempts: Ceiling on how many ALPR reads bay_state_engine queues for one visit while the plate is still unconfirmed. The truck is stationary and the camera fixed, so attempt N photographs the same obscured plate attempt 1 did; left uncapped, a truck parked for hours with an unreadable plate re-runs a full collection every cooldown window indefinitely, each one holding one of only service.num_workers threads and starving genuinely new arrivals. Only consulted by bay_state_engine -- the MQTT/HTTP trigger paths are one-shot and unaffected. Note these retries do NOT flood the enter MQTT topic: Worker.handle() recognizes a bay_state_engine-sourced job and only publishes it once the plate is actually confirmed (or never, if every attempt fails) -- a NO_VALID_PLATE result from attempt 3 of 20 is saved to disk (and to audit/all_attempts/, see save_all_attempt_frames) but not published, so a downstream consumer of the enter topic sees at most one message per visit. A one-shot MQTT/HTTP trigger's NO_VALID_PLATE is unaffected by this and still publishes as normal (still gated only by publish_no_valid_plate below).
_notes.alpr.model_load_max_retries / model_load: Each Worker thread retries loading YOLO+PaddleOCR this many times (backoff_sec apart) before giving up -- a transient failure (a network blip fetching a model file, a proxy hiccup) shouldn't need a full process restart to recover from. If every attempt still fails, that worker thread does NOT die silently the way it used to (an uncaught exception in a background thread just prints a traceback and vanishes, with nothing published anywhere and jobs left to queue forever) -- it stays alive and publishes a MODEL_LOAD_FAILED error result for every job it's handed instead, so a downstream consumer gets a signal and the cause is visible on the result topic, not just buried in a log file nobody's watching.
_notes.bay_monitor.classify_max_dimension / cla: classify_max_dimension downscales a frame so its longest side is at most this many pixels before it is JPEG-encoded and sent to the vision model (0 disables downscaling). This matters more than it looks: a vision model's prefill cost scales with pixel count, and a raw 5MP snapshot is ~6x the pixels of a 1024-wide view -- on a CPU-only box that difference routinely exceeds ollama_timeout_sec, and a timeout discards the fetch, the encode and the partial inference alike, leaving the bay with no status at all. Reference exemplars are downscaled the same way, once at startup, so they don't multiply the per-call bill.
_notes.bay_monitor.presence_diff_*: The entire baseline presence check: a small thumbnail of the ROI is compared against the one from the last time this bay was looked at while empty -- deliberately NOT the ALPR plate model (a bay is occupied or not regardless of whether a plate happens to be visible in frame). A resize+diff (~100us) is the whole cost, run every baseline_scan_interval_ms round. A change big enough to matter -- a truck arriving -- moves far more pixels than presence_diff_threshold tolerates, so this cannot miss an arrival. The cached thumbnail is cleared on both the arrival and departure transitions, so it never compares against a frame from before/after a visit. Set presence_diff_enabled to false to report presence unconditionally on every round instead (bypasses the check entirely -- useful for tuning classify_interval_sec/the prompt without waiting for an actual scene change).
_notes.bay_monitor.classify_diff_*: The same thumbnail-diff mechanism as presence_diff_*, but answering a different question: once a bay is already zoomed in, has the scene changed enough since the last classify to reclassify right now (e.g. idle -> unloading) instead of waiting out classify_interval_sec? Runs ALONGSIDE that timer, not instead of it, so a zoomed-in bay is now fetched every baseline_scan_interval_ms round (not just when the timer is due) -- a subtle change too small to trip classify_diff_threshold still gets caught on the next scheduled tick either way. Uses its own threshold, separate from presence_diff_threshold, since 'is anything here at all' and 'did an established truck's activity change' don't need the same sensitivity. Set classify_diff_enabled to false to go back to pure timer-only reclassification.
_notes.bay_monitor.ollama_think: Sent as the /api/generate 'think' field. Reasoning models (e.g. qwen3) emit a hidden 'thinking' trace before their actual answer unless told not to -- confirmed on a real deployment to cut one classify call from ~31.7s to ~6.4s once set to false. Safe to leave false even for non-reasoning models, which just ignore a field they don't recognize.
_notes.bay_monitor.save_latest_frame: Overwrites audit/<bay>/latest_frame.jpg on every successful snapshot fetch -- a live 'what does this camera see right now' view for remote troubleshooting (confirming framing/focus/ROI without direct access to the camera feed), without the volume of diagnostics_mode='troubleshooting''s per-event dumps. One file per bay, always the most recent, never accumulates.
_notes.bay_monitor.classification_prompt (STATU: The default prompt asks the vision model to answer in a fixed two-line format -- 'STATUS: <word>' then 'COMMENT: <reasoning>' -- parsed by bay_monitor.split_status_comment() into separate status and comment values BEFORE status is resolved. The COMMENT is explicitly asked for the WHY, not a restatement of the status ('cargo doors open, boxes visible on the ground' rather than just 'the bay is loading') -- that's what actually makes mqtt.bay_notification_topic_prefix's comment field useful for spot-checking a classification you don't trust, versus a comment that just repeats the status word in a sentence. Splitting also matters for correctness: without it, a comment mentioning a different status word than the one actually chosen (e.g. 'STATUS: idle / COMMENT: looks mostly empty of cargo') would make the status-matching logic see two candidate words in the same blob of text and call the whole reply too ambiguous to act on. If you override classification_prompt with your own text that doesn't ask for this format, both parts fall back to the whole raw reply -- the original single-word-only behavior -- so a custom prompt still works, it just won't have a comment to report.
_notes.mqtt.bay_event_topic_prefix / publish_ba: bay_event is the lean, consumer-facing topic and the only one published by default -- exactly the events a dock system needs, at roughly three messages per visit, against the dozens the three older bay topics emit between them. Published to bay_event_topic_prefix + '/<bay>': 'arrived' {truck_number, door_state, alert} when a truck is detected at an empty bay -- truck_number is usually the UNKNOWN placeholder this early since the ALPR read takes seconds, and alert is 'door_open_on_arrival' when the truck backed in with its doors ALREADY open, else null; 'identified' {truck_number, confidence, door_state} when that plate later resolves, and never published if the plate was already known at arrival, so there is no redundant pair; 'departed' {truck_number, door_state, duration_sec}. Requires bay_state_engine.enabled -- only it tracks truck identity. The publish_bay_* flags gate each of the four bay topics independently: publish_bay_status (bay_monitor's per-classification firehose), publish_bay_state (every session transition) and publish_bay_notification (every activity change, carrying an image) all default FALSE because between them they bury the handful of events anyone actually reacts to; turn one back on if something already consumes it. The on-demand webhook below answers everything else on request rather than by broadcasting it.
_notes.alpr.retry_only_when_plate_visible: Spend a RETRY plate read only when bay_monitor's truck model can actually see a plate in frame (its Number_Plate class). A retry costs a full collection window on one of only service.num_workers threads, and max_read_attempts is a per-VISIT budget -- so a retry fired while the plate is out of view isn't merely wasted, it makes it likelier the budget runs out before the plate ever comes INTO view. Only has any effect with bay_monitor.classifier="yolo": the ollama backend reports no plate information at all, which is treated as "go ahead" rather than "no plate", so this can never silently stop retries for a deployment not running the truck model. Gates RETRIES only -- the arrival read always fires, since entry is when a truck is most likely facing the camera and the worker polls its own frames across a whole collection window anyway. GET /bay/<bay> reports plate_visible so "no read yet because no plate is visible" can be told apart from "a plate is right there and OCR keeps failing".
_notes.alpr.abandon_read_when_doors_open: Stop trying to read a plate once bay_monitor's truck model reports the truck's doors are OPEN, and publish the observation instead -- a 'plate_unreadable' event with reason='doors_open' on the bay_event topic. The physical reason: on a reversed-in trailer the rear doors swing OUT and cover the number plate, so once they're open the plate is not in the frame at all. No amount of retrying, better OCR or a longer collection window recovers it, and every further attempt photographs a door while spending the visit's max_read_attempts budget. Published once per VISIT, not per classification, so a truck sitting with its doors open for an hour doesn't re-announce it. The ARRIVAL read still fires even for a truck that backs in with its doors already open -- it costs one attempt, it happens while the truck is still moving into position, and abandoning before ever looking would mean never reading a plate that was in fact briefly visible. Only has effect with bay_monitor.classifier='yolo': door_state is null on the ollama backend, which means no information and never abandons.
_notes.alpr.abandon_read_when_docked: A dock camera can only read a plate during a narrow window: while the truck is still coming IN, plate toward the camera. The truck model reports which side of that window it's on -- its Truck_Enter_* classes map to phase 'entering', Truck_Docked_* to phase 'docked'. Once the truck has finished reversing in, its plate faces away from the camera entirely and no amount of retrying recovers it. Confirmed in the field: every bay logging boxes_detected=0 with an empty rejected={} across 11 frames, i.e. the plate model found nothing because there was nothing to find. Reading stops at that point and a 'plate_unreadable' event with reason='docked' is published once per visit instead. If the FIRST sighting of a visit is already docked -- the entry happened between scans, or the truck model only caught it once parked -- no read is attempted at all, and the arrival event carries read_skipped='already_docked'. Only has effect with bay_monitor.classifier='yolo': phase is null on the ollama backend, meaning no information, and never closes the window.
_notes.alpr.read_startup_occupancy: Whether to run an ALPR read for a truck that was ALREADY at the bay when the service started. Default false. bay_monitor deliberately forces one classification per bay at startup to establish ground truth, which correctly finds those bays occupied and opens a session for each -- but the truck docked long before the process began, so its plate window is long gone and the read is an ~8 second collection guaranteed to return nothing, running on a worker thread that genuinely new arrivals are queueing for. This was visible in the field as a burst of boxes_detected=0 reads across every bay within the first 30 seconds of startup. The arrival is still detected and published normally, with read_skipped='startup_occupancy' on the event; only the doomed read is skipped. Set true to attempt it anyway -- e.g. a forward-facing camera where a parked truck's plate does stay visible.
_notes.alpr.read_arrival_when_doors_open: Whether a truck that backs in with its rear doors ALREADY open still gets one arrival read attempt. Default false. This originally allowed the attempt, on the reasoning that a single read is cheap insurance against a plate that happened to be briefly visible while the truck was still moving into position. Field logs settled it the other way: essentially every arrival at these bays reported doors already open, so the "rare insurance" case was actually the normal case -- and each attempt cost a full ~8.5s collection that came back boxes_detected=0 with an empty rejected={} every single time, because the open doors covered the plate from the first frame onward. The arrival is still detected, still published, and still raises alert=door_open_on_arrival; only the doomed read is skipped, with read_skipped="doors_open_on_arrival" on the event. Set true to restore the attempt (e.g. a camera angle where the plate stays visible past the open doors). Only has effect with abandon_read_when_doors_open on and bay_monitor.classifier='yolo', the only backend that reports door state.
_notes.bay_monitor.plate_assist_*: Run the dedicated plate-only model (by default the same top-level model_path weights the ALPR workers use) ALONGSIDE the truck model as a second opinion on whether anything is at the bay. The two models fail in different places -- the truck model can miss a truck at an awkward angle or in poor light, while the plate-only model is trained on one thing and often still finds the plate in exactly those frames -- so taking their UNION (a truck OR a plate counts as presence) catches entries either alone would miss. That is the whole reason to pay for a second inference per classification. It also gives a better plate_visible signal for alpr.retry_only_when_plate_visible, since the dedicated model is generally the better judge of that. When ONLY the plate model sees something, the bay is reported as plate_assist_only_status ('occupied' by default) with door_state left UNKNOWN rather than guessed -- a plate box says nothing whatsoever about a cargo door, and inventing 'closed' would feed a fabricated reading straight into the door-open-on-arrival alert. Only has effect with bay_monitor.classifier='yolo'. plate_assist_imgsz is 640 (not the truck model's 416) because a plate is a small object and needs the resolution.
_notes.model_probe (06_Model_Probe.py): A measuring instrument, not part of the service -- run it with `python 06_Model_Probe.py` and stop with Ctrl-C. It polls every enabled camera in turn, runs BOTH models on each frame (the dedicated plate model and the truck/door model), records what each one saw, and saves an annotated image whenever either finds something. It touches nothing the service owns -- no bay state, no sessions, no ALPR reads, no enter/leave results -- so it is safe to run alongside a live service or on its own. Two deliberate differences from the production pipeline, both because matching it would corrupt the measurement: it applies NO geometry filters (the alpr.too_small/upper_half/off_center rules discarded ALL 11 boxes on a bay where the plate model was working perfectly, so a probe reproducing them would report zero and hide exactly what it exists to find), and it probes the FULL FRAME by default (use_roi true to compare) because a mis-placed ROI looks identical to a blind model when you only see the filtered result. Output goes to audit/<output_subdir>/: detections.jsonl (one JSON object per frame, the analysis source of truth), summary.json (running totals per bay and overall, rewritten as it goes so it is readable mid-run), and images/ -- every annotated frame from every bay in ONE flat folder, named <bay>_<timestamp>_p<plate-model boxes>_t<trucks>_tp<truck-model plates>.jpg, so a single sorted listing groups each camera chronologically and shows which model found what without opening anything (a per-bay folder tree meant opening one directory per camera to review a run). Box colours: GREEN = the dedicated plate model, BLUE = the truck model’s truck classes, YELLOW = the truck model’s own Number_Plate class -- where green and yellow disagree is the direct A/B between the two. save_images picks which frames get an image written: "classes" (the default) saves only frames where the truck model reported one of save_classes -- defaulted to the two ENTERING classes, since entry is the only moment a dock camera can read a plate and a run full of docked-truck frames is mostly noise when that is the question. The other modes are "any" (either model saw anything), "plate", "truck", "all" (every frame) and "none" (JSONL only). save_classes is matched case-insensitively against the truck model's class names, its plate class included, so "Number_Plate" may be listed too. Note that detections.jsonl still records EVERY frame from both models whatever save_images is set to -- the filter only governs which frames get a jpg, so narrowing it never costs measurement data. max_saved_images_per_bay caps disk use (0 = unlimited). The log prints a periodic SUMMARY with the agreement counts that settle the question -- how often each model sees something the other misses -- plus a final one on Ctrl-C. plate_model_path and truck_model_path default to the models the service already uses (model_path and bay_monitor.truck_model_path). Confidence thresholds default LOWER than production (0.25) on purpose: the probe is measuring what each model can see at all, and a high threshold would hide marginal detections that are exactly what needs judging.
_notes.model_probe.ocr_*: Turns the probe from a detector into a reader. A valid ENTRY opens a plate-reading session for that bay, and every LATER frame’s plate boxes are OCR’d into it until one passes plate_text.is_valid() or the budget runs out. Reading across frames rather than once is the point: a single crop of a moving truck is often motion-blurred or half-turned, and the probe is already polling that bay every couple of seconds. ocr_trigger_classes opens a session on a truck of that class that ALSO passes the enter_max_bottom_px geometry test -- Truck_Enter_Closed by default, since doors-closed is exactly when the plate is not covered by them; a docked truck mislabelled Enter is rejected first, so the reader never spends its budget on a plate facing away from the camera. ocr_trigger_on_plate additionally opens a session whenever either model detects a plate at all, which catches entries the truck model misses entirely. Both models’ plate boxes get read, since either can see one the other misses. Crops are padded by ocr_crop_padding_pct on each side (a slightly undersized box clips a character off the plate edge -- confirmed in the field) and near-identical repeats are skipped so a stationary truck cannot burn the attempt budget re-reading the same pixels. Results publish to ocr_topic_prefix + "/<bay>", INCLUDING the failures -- {bay, status: READ|NO_VALID_PLATE|TIMEOUT, plate, confidence, raw, trigger, attempts, frames, elapsed_sec, reads[]} -- because "a truck entered and its plate could not be read" is a result worth knowing, not silence. The winning crop is written to audit/<output_subdir>/plates/ as <bay>_<timestamp>_<plate>.jpg. Set ocr_enabled false to skip loading PaddleOCR entirely when only detection counts are wanted.
_notes.model_probe.enter_max_bottom_px / enter_: Geometric test for whether a truck is really ENTERING or is a docked one the model labelled Enter -- confirmed in the field, where clearly-docked trucks came back as Truck_Enter_Open and Truck_Enter_Closed at both high and low confidence, so filtering by class alone still filled the images folder with parked trucks. One line across the frame does it: a valid entry’s bounding box must not reach further DOWN than that line. A truck that has finished reversing in sits right against the dock, and so against the bottom of the frame, which pushes its box bottom past the line; one still approaching is further away and its box ends higher up. Decided from the same single frame, with no history kept. enter_max_bottom_px WINS when set, because that is how the line is actually measured -- read straight off a frame, in the same pixel coordinates the boxes use: 1600 on these 2592x1944 cameras, i.e. the bottom edge must stay above y=1600 of 1944. enter_max_bottom_frac (0.75) is the resolution-independent fallback used only when the pixel value is 0/null; setting both to 0 disables the check entirely. Applies to TRUCK boxes only when save_images="classes" -- plate boxes are not gated, since the rule is about how far down a truck reaches and a plate is small and low by nature. A box landing exactly on the line is accepted. Every box’s bottom edge is recorded in detections.jsonl in BOTH forms (box[3] in pixels and bottom_frac as a fraction of frame height) whatever gets saved, so the threshold can be re-picked from real recorded data rather than guessed.
_notes.bay_monitor.classifier / truck_*: Which backend answers 'what is happening at this bay'. 'yolo' uses a purpose-trained truck/door detection model at truck_model_path (resolved relative to config.json, like model_path); roughly 50ms per frame, deterministic, and it reports door state, which the vision model never did reliably. The speed matters beyond the obvious: bay_monitor scans every bay from ONE thread, so a multi-second vision-model call does not just delay that bay, it stalls the round-robin for every bay queued behind it -- and a timing-out call leaves a bay with no status at all (activity: null) indefinitely. 'ollama' is the original vision-model prompt (classification_prompt + status_values + reference_images). The vision model stays reachable either way for on-demand questions (POST /bay/<bay>/ask), which is what it is actually good at: 'loading or unloading?' is not something a fixed detector vocabulary can answer. Built-in class mapping is Truck_Enter_Closed->arriving/closed, Truck_Enter_Open->arriving/open, Truck_Docked_Closed->docked/closed, Truck_Docked_Open->loading/open; Number_Plate (truck_plate_class) is reported as plate_visible but NEVER counts as truck presence, since a bay is occupied whether or not a plate happens to be readable from the dock camera's angle. truck_class_map overrides/extends that mapping for a model retrained with different class names, merged over the built-in map so a partial override does not silently drop the rest. truck_imgsz is 416 rather than 640 because trucks are large objects filling much of the frame -- raise it if small or distant trucks are missed. Startup fails loudly if classifier is 'yolo' and the weights are missing, rather than reporting every bay empty forever.
_notes.bay_monitor.door_state_debounce_count: Consecutive agreeing frames before a door-state CHANGE is believed, same reasoning as empty_debounce_count -- a half-raised shutter or someone walking through the doorway should not flip the reported state. This affects only the debounced state that GET /bay/<bay> reports; the door_open_on_arrival alert deliberately uses the raw reading from the arrival frame itself, since 'did this truck arrive with its doors open' is a claim about one specific moment and waiting several frames to confirm it would answer a different question.
_notes.bay_monitor.attach_frame_to_status: Whether the truck-model backend also base64-encodes each classified frame for downstream payloads. Pure overhead unless something actually ships the image, so it defaults to whatever mqtt.publish_bay_notification is set to. The ollama backend always has an encoded frame regardless -- it had to build one to make the call at all.
_notes.bay_monitor.snapshot_webhook_*: Pull, not push: nothing is sent anywhere on a timer. When snapshot_webhook_enabled is true, a separate small HTTP server (waitress, like http_trigger's) listens on snapshot_webhook_host:snapshot_webhook_port and answers GET /snapshot/<bay> with {bay, occupancy_status, activity, image_base64, timestamp} on request. Serves audit/<bay>/latest_frame.jpg (requires bay_monitor.save_latest_frame, default true) -- already at most one baseline_scan_interval_ms round stale (2s by default) -- rather than fetching a brand new frame per request, so it never contends with bay_monitor's own camera session. occupancy_status/activity report this bay's last-known classification, both null until it's been classified at least once; 404 if the bay is unrecognized or nothing's been saved for it yet. Separate server/port from http_trigger on purpose -- receiving camera alerts and serving snapshots-on-request are unrelated concerns. The served image is downscaled to snapshot_webhook_max_dimension on its longest side (640 by default -- 640x480 from a 4:3 camera, 640x360 from a 16:9 one, aspect ratio always preserved) and re-encoded at snapshot_webhook_jpeg_quality, since full camera resolution would make a multi-megabyte JSON body out of what is normally wanted as a thumbnail; the response carries the actual width/height served, and max_dimension 0 serves the frame at original size. These are separate from classify_max_dimension/classify_jpeg_quality (what the vision model is shown) on purpose -- retuning a dashboard thumbnail shouldn't change what gets classified.
_notes.alpr.save_detected_plate_frames: On every SUCCESS result, copies the crop that actually produced the winning plate into a separate, flat audit/detected_plates/ folder (named '<timestamp>_<bay>_<direction>_<plate>.jpg') -- so confirmed reads can be browsed chronologically at a glance across all bays, without hunting through each job's own per-event audit subfolder. The full per-job detail (result.json, every candidate crop) is still written to its usual per-event folder either way.
_notes.alpr.save_all_attempt_frames: On EVERY completed job -- SUCCESS or not -- copies the best-scoring attempted crop into a separate, flat audit/all_attempts/ folder (named '<timestamp>_<bay>_<direction>_<status>_<plate-or-UNKNOWN>.jpg'). Different question from save_detected_plate_frames above (which only ever shows confirmed reads): this is 'what is the camera actually seeing, why is this bay coming back NO_VALID_PLATE' -- browse one folder chronologically instead of opening each job's own nested audit subfolder one at a time. With bay_state_engine retrying a stubborn plate many times per visit, this is usually the fastest way to see what's actually going wrong.

bay_monitor.classification_prompt:
You are monitoring a truck loading dock bay through a fixed security camera. Classify the current activity into EXACTLY ONE of these words: empty, occupied, unloading, loading, idle. 'empty' = no truck present. 'occupied' = a truck is present but no cargo movement is visible. 'unloading' = cargo is visibly being removed from the truck. 'loading' = cargo is visibly being loaded onto the truck. 'idle' = a truck is present, not actively loading or unloading (e.g. waiting, doors closed, driver break). Respond in EXACTLY this two-line format, nothing else:
STATUS: <the single classification word>
COMMENT: <briefly explain WHY you chose that status -- the specific visual evidence you reasoned from (e.g. cargo doors open/closed, boxes or pallets visible on the ground or being carried, a forklift or workers present, the truck bed's visible contents), not just a restatement of the status word>
